body.statement: There are constants \(C_1,C_2<\infty\), depending only on \(s,M,v,\alpha\), such that if \(T_n\ge C_1\log(e/\kappa_n)\), then \(I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}\) is uniformly honest over \(\mathcal P_n\) and \[\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}E_P[|I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}|]\le C_2\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}.\] Consequently \(L_n(\kappa_n)\asymp L_n^{\mathrm{known}}(\kappa_n)\) in this region, uniformly over vanishing \(\kappa_n\). This strictly extends the fixed-jump oracle conclusion of Porter and Yu (2015) by allowing \(\kappa_n\to0\) down to the stated boundary and by delivering uniform honest connected-interval length.
body.justification: This theorem now supplies a completely evaluable honest procedure and oracle expected-length guarantee at the Lipschitz endpoint, with all grids, thresholds, fallbacks, and constants displayed.
body.gap: Known-cutoff weak-first-stage inference and fixed-jump unknown-cutoff oracle substitution do not imply uniform honest connected-length attainment when the jump vanishes.  The theorem closes that gap for \(s=1\); a slope-kink witness shows why the prescribed scan cannot close it for \(s>1\) under the same class.
body.consumer: For Lipschitz reduced forms, researchers can implement the four-fold rule and recover the known-cutoff length whenever \(n\kappa_n^3\) exceeds the logarithmic location-search cost.
body.proof_tex:
We prove the narrowed statement at \(s=1\).  In this case
\[
 H=\frac{\kappa_n}{2^{12}M},\qquad
 b=m^{-1/3},\qquad
 T_n=n\kappa_n^3,\qquad
 \rho_n=n^{-1/3}.
 \tag{8}
\]
Put
\[
 L_\alpha=\log(32/\alpha),\qquad
 A_\alpha=2^{16}L_\alpha,
\]
\[
 B_{M,\alpha}
 =1+\log\!\left(\frac{16(1+2^{17}M)}{\alpha}\right),
\]
and define the following finite constants:
\[
 C_r
 =8M+16A_\alpha+1+16M(A_\alpha+1)+8\sqrt{L_\alpha},
\]
\[
 c_3=2^{-24}M^{-1},\qquad c_2=2^{-22},
\]
\[
 C_F
 =2(3e c_3)^{-1/3}+12(2e c_2)^{-1/2},
 \qquad
 C_2=16C_r+4C_F,
\]
and
\[
 C_1=\max\left\{
 2^{27}MB_{M,\alpha},\;
 2^{15}M(8A_\alpha+1),\;
 8(8C_r)^3,\;
 2^{30}ML_\alpha
 \right\}.
 \tag{9}
\]
These displayed choices are not optimized; their role is to make every
deterministic and probability inequality below simultaneous.

For sufficiently large \(n\), \(m\ge n/8\).  Since
\(N_H\le1+2^{17}M/\kappa_n\),
\[
 \log(16N_H/\alpha)
 \le B_{M,\alpha}\log(e/\kappa_n).
 \tag{10}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 2^{-11}mH\kappa_n^2
 \ge\frac{T_n}{2^{26}M}.
 \tag{11}
\]
Thus the first term in (9), the signal condition, and the localization
lemma imply
\[
 P(\mathcal E_1^c)\le\alpha/8.
 \tag{12}
\]
The same lemma, with
\(R_c=A_\alpha/(m\kappa_n^2)+1/n\), gives
\[
 P\bigl(\{|\widehat c-c_P|>R_c\}\cap\mathcal E_1\bigr)
 \le9e^{-L_\alpha}=\frac{9\alpha}{32}.
 \tag{13}
\]
Here \(R_c\ge16/n\), because \(m\le n/4\),
\(\kappa_n\le1/8\), and \(A_\alpha>1\).

We next check the two deterministic fallbacks.  Let
\(q=\kappa_n/b\).  Since \(b^{-3}=m\) and \(m\ge n/8\),
\[
 q^3=m\kappa_n^3\ge T_n/8.
 \tag{14}
\]
For \(q\ge1\), direct substitution into the definition of \(r_n\)
and \(1/n\le1/(4m)=b^3/4\) yields
\[
 r_n
 \le C_rb.
 \tag{15}
\]
Indeed, the four terms, divided by \(b\), are bounded respectively by
\(8M\), \(16A_\alpha+1\), \(16M(A_\alpha+1)\), and
\(8\sqrt{L_\alpha}\).  Equations (9), (14), and (15) give
\(r_n\le\kappa_n/8\).  Also
\[
 \frac{R_c}{H}
 =2^{12}M\left\{
 \frac{A_\alpha}{m\kappa_n^3}+\frac{1}{n\kappa_n}
 \right\}
 \le\frac{2^{12}M(8A_\alpha+1)}{T_n}
 \le\frac18,
 \tag{16}
\]
where \(n\kappa_n\ge n\kappa_n^3=T_n\).  Thus the signal condition
forces both deterministic checks in the definition to pass.

We now prove honesty.  Fix \(P\in\mathcal P_n\), and abbreviate
\(\theta=\theta_P\).  The identifying proposition and binary potential
outcomes imply \(|\theta|\le1\) and
\(y_P-\theta d_P=0\).  Consequently the conditional regression of
\(U=Y-\theta D\), separately on the two sides of \(c_P\), is
\(2M\)-Lipschitz and has zero level jump.  Gluing the two pieces at
their common value makes it globally \(2M\)-Lipschitz.  Conditional on
folds one through three, \(\widehat c\) is fixed and fold four remains
independent by \(\textnormal{ass:iid-sampling}\).  On
\(|\widehat c-c_P|\le R_c\), therefore,
\[
 \left|E_P\left[
 \widehat y(\widehat c)-\theta\widehat d(\widehat c)
 \mid F_1,F_2,F_3\right]\right|
 \le2Mb.
 \tag{17}
\]
For treatment, (1)--(3), now at bandwidth \(b\), give
\[
 \left|E_P[\widehat d(\widehat c)\mid F_1,F_2,F_3]-d_P\right|
 \le Mb+\frac{2\kappa_nR_c}{b}+2MR_c.
 \tag{18}
\]
All divisions in (18) are legitimate because \(b>0\).  Moreover, the
nonnegative term \(16\kappa_nR_c/b\) in \(r_n\), together with
\(r_n\le\kappa_n/8\), gives \(R_c/b\le1/128\), so the shift lies inside
the kernel window.

The fold-four summands are bounded and are nonzero only on a set of
\(X\)-probability \(2b\).  Here \(|U|\le2\), so the conditional second
moment is at most \(8\|K_0\|_\infty^2/b\) for \(U\), and it is at most
\(2\|K_0\|_\infty^2/b\) for \(D\).  Applying the same exponential
calculation as in (5), conditionally on the first three folds, gives
\[
 \left|\widehat\Delta_{4,b}^{U}(\widehat c)
       -E_P[\widehat\Delta_{4,b}^{U}(\widehat c)\mid F_1,F_2,F_3]
 \right|
 \le8\|K_0\|_\infty\sqrt{\frac{L_\alpha}{mb}},
 \tag{19}
\]
and the analogous inequality with constant four for \(D\), except on
an event of probability at most \(\alpha/8\).  The linear Bernstein term
is absorbed by the displayed square-root terms for all sufficiently
large \(n\), because \(mb\to\infty\).  Combining (17)--(19) with the
definition of \(r_n\) shows
\[
 \left|\widehat y(\widehat c)-
       \theta_P\widehat d(\widehat c)\right|\le2r_n.
 \tag{20}
\]
If the empirical denominator is below \(\kappa_n/2\), the rule returns
\(\Theta\), which contains \(\theta_P\); otherwise (20) puts
\(\theta_P\) in the inverted set.  By (12), (13), and (19), the failure
probability is at most
\[
 \frac\alpha8+\frac{9\alpha}{32}+\frac\alpha8
 =\frac{17\alpha}{32}<\alpha.
\]
The bound does not depend on \(P\), proving uniform honesty.

It remains to control expected length rather than only coverage.  If
\(\widehat d(\widehat c)\ge\kappa_n/2\), the accepted labels form an
interval of length at most
\[
 \frac{4r_n}{\widehat d(\widehat c)}
 \le\frac{8r_n}{\kappa_n}.
 \tag{21}
\]
On the event \(|\widehat c-c_P|\le b/8\), (18), the inequality
\(Mb\le r_n/8\le\kappa_n/64\), and a fold-four treatment fluctuation
of at most \(\kappa_n/8\) imply
\(\widehat d(\widehat c)>\kappa_n/2\).  Hence the full-length fallback
event is contained in a coarse-scan failure, a localization error larger
than \(b/8\), or a fold-four deviation larger than \(\kappa_n/8\).
Equations (5), (10)--(14), and the localization lemma consequently give
\[
 P\{\widehat d(\widehat c)<\kappa_n/2\}
 \le2e^{-c_3q^3}+12e^{-c_2q^2}.
 \tag{22}
\]
The elementary optimizations
\[
 \sup_{q\ge1}q e^{-c_3q^3}\le(3ec_3)^{-1/3},
 \qquad
 \sup_{q\ge1}q e^{-c_2q^2}\le(2ec_2)^{-1/2}
\]
turn (22) into
\[
 P\{\widehat d(\widehat c)<\kappa_n/2\}
 \le C_F\frac{b}{\kappa_n}.
 \tag{23}
\]
Since \(m\ge n/8\), \(b\le2\rho_n\).  Taking expectations in (21),
using length at most two on the fallback, and applying (15) and (23),
gives
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}E_P|I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}|
 \le\frac{8C_rb}{\kappa_n}
      +\frac{2C_Fb}{\kappa_n}
 \le C_2\frac{\rho_n}{\kappa_n}.
 \tag{24}
\]
By (14) and (9), \(\rho_n/\kappa_n<1\) in the asserted region, so the
right side of (24) is exactly of the claimed
\(\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}\) order.

Finally, every unknown-cutoff interval rule induces a known-cutoff rule
that ignores the supplied \(c_P\).  Therefore
\(L_n^{\mathrm{known}}(\kappa_n)\le L_n(\kappa_n)\).  The already proved
known-cutoff benchmark and (24) imply
\[
 c_0\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}
 \le L_n^{\mathrm{known}}(\kappa_n)
 \le L_n(\kappa_n)
 \le C_2\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}.
\]
This proves oracle-order attainment and completes the proof.
